question: Where did Job reside, and what fourfold spiritual characterization did Scripture ascribe to his moral integrity?
opt1: In the land of Uz; he was perfect and upright, one that feared God, and eschewed evil
opt2: In the land of Midian; he was righteous and meek, walking before God, and loving mercy
opt3: In the land of Edom; he was blameless and faithful, offering sacrifices, and rebuking wickedness
opt4: In the plains of Mamre; he was just and holy, keeping the covenant, and rejecting false gods
correct: In the land of Uz; he was perfect and upright, one that feared God, and eschewed evil
explanation: Job resided in the land of Uz (associated with Edom/Northern Arabia) and was characterized by supreme integrity: perfect (blameless), upright, God-fearing, and abstaining from every form of evil. Job 1:1 (KJV) - "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil."

question: What was the inventory of Job's family and immense livestock wealth, ranking him as the greatest of all men of the east?
opt1: Twelve sons, two daughters, 10,000 sheep, 2,000 camels, 1,000 oxen, 300 she asses, and five hundred servants
opt2: Seven sons, three daughters, 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 she asses, and a very great household
opt3: Five sons, five daughters, 5,000 sheep, 4,000 camels, 600 oxen, 400 she asses, and forty tents of herdsmen
opt4: Ten sons, three daughters, 8,000 sheep, 1,500 camels, 700 oxen, 800 she asses, and royal vineyards
correct: Seven sons, three daughters, 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, 500 she asses, and a very great household
explanation: Job possessed vast pastoral wealth representing the pinnacle of patriarchal prosperity in antiquity. Job 1:2-3 (KJV) - "And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters. His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east."

question: What priestly intercession did Job continually practice on behalf of his children following their cycles of feasting?
opt1: He gathered his family for three days of fasting and required each son to confess his faults before the elders
opt2: He sprinkled the blood of a bullock upon the doorposts of their houses and commanded forty days of ritual cleansing
opt3: He rose up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all, concerned they might have sinned and cursed God in their hearts
opt4: He paid a tenth of all feast expenses to the local sanctuary and dedicated his firstborn son to lifelong service
correct: He rose up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all, concerned they might have sinned and cursed God in their hearts
explanation: Job functioned as family priest, proactively offering individual burnt offerings for each child lest they harbored inadvertent irreverence in their hearts. Job 1:5 (KJV) - "And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually."

question: When the sons of God presented themselves before the LORD, what was Satan's reply regarding where he had been?
opt1: "From roaming through the wilderness of Edom seeking whom I may accuse."
opt2: "From testing the kings of the nations and observing the wickedness of mortals."
opt3: "From inspecting the four corners of heaven and the depths of the sea."
opt4: "From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it."
correct: "From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it."
explanation: Satan described his roving surveillance across the terrestrial realm, searching for vulnerabilities in humankind. Job 1:7 (KJV) - "And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it."

question: With what cynical accusation did Satan challenge Job's piety before the LORD?
opt1: He asked, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" arguing that God had hedged him about, blessed his substance, and that he would curse God to His face if his possessions were touched
opt2: He argued that Job worshipped false gods in secret and only gave outward lip service to Yahweh
opt3: He claimed that Job exacted usury from his laborers and oppressed the fatherless in the gate
opt4: He asserted that Job's righteousness was counterfeit because his sons lived in drunken revelry
correct: He asked, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" arguing that God had hedged him about, blessed his substance, and that he would curse God to His face if his possessions were touched
explanation: Satan argued that Job's devotion was purely mercenary, bought by divine protection ('a hedge') and prosperity, claiming adversity would make Job curse God to His face. Job 1:9-11 (KJV) - "Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face."

question: What precise divine boundary did the LORD place upon Satan in his first assault against Job?
opt1: Satan was permitted to take Job's cattle, but forbidden to touch his children or his dwelling
opt2: All that Job had was placed in Satan's power, but upon Job himself he was forbidden to put forth his hand
opt3: Satan was granted thirty days to test Job, but forbidden to destroy his sheep and camels
opt4: Satan was allowed to afflict his servants, but forbidden to enter the borders of Uz
correct: All that Job had was placed in Satan's power, but upon Job himself he was forbidden to put forth his hand
explanation: God established sovereign limits: Satan could destroy Job's possessions and family, but was barred from touching Job's physical body. Job 1:12 (KJV) - "And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD."

question: What were the first two catastrophic reports delivered by sole surviving messengers to Job in a single day?
opt1: Chaldeans plundered the sheep; then an earthquake swallowed the asses and fifty servants
opt2: Amalekites raided the camels; then a plague of locusts devoured the agricultural crops
opt3: Sabeans fell upon the oxen and she asses, slaying the servants; then the fire of God fell from heaven, burning up the sheep and servants
opt4: Philistines stole the oxen; then lightning struck the storehouses of grain
correct: Sabeans fell upon the oxen and she asses, slaying the servants; then the fire of God fell from heaven, burning up the sheep and servants
explanation: Disasters struck back-to-back: Sabean marauders took the plowing oxen and asses, followed by supernatural fire ('fire of God') consuming the 7,000 sheep. Job 1:14-16 (KJV) - "And there came a messenger unto Job, and said, The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them: And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee."

question: What were the final two devastating reports that completed the total ruin of Job's substance and family?
opt1: Syrian raiders captured the camels; then a flood of the river Jordan swept away the feast tent with all his sons
opt2: Midianite bands plundered the camels; then a fire in the banquet hall suffocated all his children
opt3: Edomite cavalry seized the camels; then a pestilence struck down all ten children in one hour
opt4: Chaldeans in three bands carried away the camels and slew the servants; then a great desert wind collapsed the eldest brother's house, killing all ten of Job's children
correct: Chaldeans in three bands carried away the camels and slew the servants; then a great desert wind collapsed the eldest brother's house, killing all ten of Job's children
explanation: The Chaldean raid eliminated the 3,000 camels, and a desert whirlwind crushed the house where his 10 children were gathered, killing them all. Job 1:17-19 (KJV) - "While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house: And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee."

question: How did Job respond physically and spiritually upon hearing of the death of his children and the loss of all his possessions?
opt1: He arose, rent his mantle, shaved his head, fell down upon the ground, and worshipped
opt2: He cried out in bitter curses against the Sabeans and collapsed unconscious in the dust
opt3: He built an altar of twelve unhewn stones, offered forty rams, and rebuked the messengers
opt4: He rent his robes, wept before the elders of Uz, and demanded an audience with God
correct: He arose, rent his mantle, shaved his head, fell down upon the ground, and worshipped
explanation: Job expressed deep Oriental grief (tearing mantle, shaving head) yet channeled his agony into prostrate worship of the sovereign Creator. Job 1:20 (KJV) - "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped,"

question: With what immortal confession of faith and divine sovereignty did Job conclude his response to total loss, and what verdict did Scripture record?
opt1: "The LORD is my strength and shield; my heart trusted in Him and I am helped." In all this Job wept without bitterness
opt2: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly
opt3: "Though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him: He also shall be my salvation." In all this Job maintained his righteous defense
opt4: "Shall a man receive prosperity and not adversity from the Maker?" In all this Job confessed his hidden iniquities
correct: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly
explanation: Job acknowledged divine ownership of all life and goods, praising God in the face of ruin; the inspired text certifies he did not sin or charge God foolishly. Job 1:21-22 (KJV) - "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly."

question: When the sons of God assembled again, what divine commendation did the LORD proclaim concerning Job's steadfast integrity?
opt1: That Job had offered seventy bullocks to atone for the sins of the land of Uz
opt2: That Job still held fast his integrity, although Satan had moved God against him to destroy him without cause
opt3: That Job had silenced the mockers of Edom through his exemplary fasting
opt4: That Job was worthy to receive double recompense immediately for his faithfulness
correct: That Job still held fast his integrity, although Satan had moved God against him to destroy him without cause
explanation: God vindicated Job before the angelic host, noting that despite unprovoked ruin ('without cause'), Job remained immovably upright. Job 2:3 (KJV) - "And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause."

question: What cynical proverb did Satan employ to demand a second, more severe physical trial against Job?
opt1: "A living dog is better than a dead lion; strike his eyes with blindness and he will blaspheme thy throne."
opt2: "Blood for blood, tooth for tooth; afflict his body with leprosy and his faith will turn to dust."
opt3: "Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life. But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face."
opt4: "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak; crush his bones in the night and he will deny his Creator."
correct: "Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life. But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face."
explanation: Satan claimed Job tolerated property loss because his own flesh was spared; striking his physical health, he insisted, would force Job to curse God. Job 2:4-5 (KJV) - "And Satan answered the LORD, and said, Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life. But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face."

question: What explicit restriction did the LORD impose upon Satan when delivering Job into his hands for the second trial?
opt1: "Behold, thou mayest afflict him, but touch not his tongue or his lips."
opt2: "Thou hast power over his flesh, but spare his sight and his reason."
opt3: "He is in thy power for seven months; then shall his healing spring forth."
opt4: "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life."
correct: "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life."
explanation: Satan's power was strictly bounded by divine sovereignty: he could afflict Job's body to the brink of death, but could not take his life. Job 2:6 (KJV) - "And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life."

question: With what gruesome physical affliction did Satan strike Job from head to foot?
opt1: With sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown
opt2: With incurable white leprosy that withered his limbs
opt3: With burning fiery ulcers and blindness in both eyes
opt4: With black gangrene and consumption of the lungs
correct: With sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown
explanation: Satan afflicted Job with malignant, excruciating ulcers (sore boils) covering his entire body without a single spared spot. Job 2:7 (KJV) - "So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown."

question: What crude instrument did Job use to scrape his weeping ulcers, and where did he sit in his misery?
opt1: He used a sharp flint knife and sat outside the city gate in sackcloth
opt2: He took a potsherd (broken piece of pottery) to scrape himself withal, and sat down among the ashes
opt3: He used an iron scraper and knelt beside the dried-up brook
opt4: He used a piece of cedar wood and lay prostrate upon his bed of straw
correct: He took a potsherd (broken piece of pottery) to scrape himself withal, and sat down among the ashes
explanation: Job sought relief from itching and suppuration using a broken shard of earthenware, sitting on the public ash-heap (dunghill) outside the settlement. Job 2:8 (KJV) - "And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes."

question: What despairing counsel did Job's wife urge upon him in his agonizing affliction?
opt1: "Why sittest thou in the dust? Repent of thy secret sins that God may heal thee."
opt2: "Flee unto the mountains of Edom, for our house is desolate and our name forgotten."
opt3: "Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die."
opt4: "Demand an answer of the Almighty, for He hath dealt unjustly with our household."
correct: "Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die."
explanation: Overwhelmed by grief and horror at his suffering, Job's wife urged him to abandon his integrity, renounce God, and accept death. Job 2:9 (KJV) - "Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die."

question: With what profound theological reply did Job rebuke his wife, preserving his righteousness?
opt1: He said, "Get thee behind me, for thou savourest not the things of God." In all this Job held his peace
opt2: He said, "God is righteous in all His ways, and I will not blaspheme." In all this Job wept bitterly
opt3: He said, "The Almighty shall vindicate my cause in the day of judgment." In all this Job offered incense
opt4: He said, "Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this did not Job sin with his lips
correct: He said, "Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this did not Job sin with his lips
explanation: Job refused to adopt a conditional faith that only welcomes blessings, recognizing God's absolute sovereignty over both prosperity and adversity. Job 2:10 (KJV) - "But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips."

question: Who were the three friends of Job who made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and comfort him?
opt1: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite
opt2: Elihu the Buzite, Barachel the Ramite, and Hiram the Tyrian
opt3: Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and Tattenai the governor
opt4: Jethro the Midianite, Balaam the son of Beor, and Melchizedek of Salem
correct: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite
explanation: Job's three companions represented ancient wisdom centers: Teman (famed for wisdom, Jer 49:7), Shuah (descendants of Abraham via Keturah, Gen 25:2), and Naamah. Job 2:11 (KJV) - "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him."

question: How did Job's three friends react when they saw him from a distance, disfigured by disease?
opt1: They covered their faces in horror, turned away from the ash-heap, and refused to draw near
opt2: They knew him not; they lifted up their voice and wept, rent their mantles, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven
opt3: They fell to the ground crying out for mercy, offering sacrifices upon three stone altars
opt4: They examined his ulcers and immediately rebuked him for unconfessed generational wickedness
correct: They knew him not; they lifted up their voice and wept, rent their mantles, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven
explanation: His physical disfigurement was so extreme they did not recognize him, prompting visceral lamentation with weeping, torn garments, and casting dust toward heaven. Job 2:12 (KJV) - "And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven."

question: For what duration did the three friends sit in complete silence with Job upon the ground, and why did none speak a word?
opt1: Three days and three nights; none spoke because Persian mourning laws forbade speech
opt2: Forty days and forty nights; none spoke until Job should break his fast
opt3: Seven days and seven nights; none spake a word unto him, for they saw that his grief was very great
opt4: Twelve days and nights; none spoke because they were terrified of contracting his disease
correct: Seven days and seven nights; none spake a word unto him, for they saw that his grief was very great
explanation: The friends observed the traditional 7-day mourning period (cf. Gen 50:10) in profound empathetic silence, stunned by the unfathomable depth of Job's agony. Job 2:13 (KJV) - "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."

question: When Job finally broke the seven-day silence in Chapter 3, what did he open his mouth to curse?
opt1: He cursed the Sabeans and Chaldeans who destroyed his wealth
opt2: He cursed the adversary Satan who smote him with boils
opt3: He cursed his day (the day of his birth)
opt4: He cursed the name of the Almighty for bringing affliction
correct: He cursed his day (the day of his birth)
explanation: Job never cursed God (which Satan predicted), but in raw poetic anguish, he cursed the very day he entered human existence. Job 3:1 (KJV) - "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day."

question: With what poetic lament did Job curse his nativity in Job 3:3?
opt1: "Cursed be the hour that saw my mother's travail, and the day that cradled my youth."
opt2: "Let darkness cover the foundations of Uz, and let the sun hide its face from my generation."
opt3: "Why did the dawn awaken upon my cradle, and why was my name written among the living?"
opt4: "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived."
correct: "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived."
explanation: Job wished non-existence upon both his birth-day and the night of his conception. Job 3:3 (KJV) - "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived."

question: Whom did Job summon to cast darkness upon the night of his birth in Job 3:8?
opt1: Those who curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning (or arouse Leviathan)
opt2: The watchmen of the night who guard the city walls
opt3: The Chaldean astrologers who read the eclipse of the stars
opt4: The mourners of Edom who blow the rams' horns at dusk
correct: Those who curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning (or arouse Leviathan)
explanation: Job poetically invoked professional enchanters or mythical mourners capable of rousing Leviathan (the chaotic sea monster) to engulf his birth-night in perpetual darkness. Job 3:8 (KJV) - "Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning."

question: What agonized questions did Job utter concerning his survival at birth in Job 3:11-12?
opt1: "Why did the midwife deliver my soul? why was I not buried beneath the threshold of my father's house?"
opt2: "Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck?"
opt3: "Why did the light shine upon mine eyes? why did I not perish in the desert like water spilled upon sand?"
opt4: "Why was my breath preserved for calamity? why did my mother rejoice over a son of sorrows?"
correct: "Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck?"
explanation: Job questioned why maternal care ('knees' to receive, 'breasts' to nourish) welcomed him into life rather than allowing stillbirth. Job 3:11-12 (KJV) - "Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck?"

question: With whom did Job contemplate that he would have rested in peaceful stillness had he died at birth?
opt1: With the righteous patriarchs who walked with God before the flood
opt2: With the angels of heaven who sing perpetual praises around the throne
opt3: With kings and counselors of the earth who built desolate places (pyramids/tombs) for themselves, and princes that had gold and filled their houses with silver
opt4: With his ten deceased children who slept beneath the dust of the wilderness
correct: With kings and counselors of the earth who built desolate places (pyramids/tombs) for themselves, and princes that had gold and filled their houses with silver
explanation: Job viewed death as the great leveler where he would share tranquil slumber alongside monarchs, empire-builders, and wealthy dignitaries. Job 3:13-15 (KJV) - "For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves; Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver:"

question: How did Job portray the peace and absolute equality of the realm of the dead (Sheol) in Job 3:17-19?
opt1: There the righteous reign on golden thrones, while the wicked suffer eternal torment in unquenchable fire
opt2: There the rich give account of their stewardship, and the poor inherit fertile pastures beside living waters
opt3: There all memory of earth is wiped away, and mortals drink of the river of forgetfulness
opt4: There the wicked cease from troubling; the weary be at rest; prisoners rest together without hearing the oppressor's voice; the small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master
correct: There the wicked cease from troubling; the weary be at rest; prisoners rest together without hearing the oppressor's voice; the small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master
explanation: Job described death as a sanctuary from earthly oppression: absolute cessation of malice, relief for the exhausted, and freedom for enslaved captives. Job 3:17-19 (KJV) - "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest. There the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor. The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master."

question: How did Job describe the intense yearning for death felt by those in hopeless physical and emotional misery?
opt1: They long for death, but it cometh not; they dig for it more than for hid treasures; and rejoice exceedingly when they can find the grave
opt2: They weep at midnight for the angel of the end, but their prayers are turned away like smoke
opt3: They seek refuge in the deep caves of the mountains, yet the sun finds them in their sorrow
opt4: They cry out for the sword of the enemy, but even the marauders pass them by in pity
correct: They long for death, but it cometh not; they dig for it more than for hid treasures; and rejoice exceedingly when they can find the grave
explanation: Job captured the agony of persistent suffering: searching for death with greater eagerness than miners digging for precious buried treasure. Job 3:21-22 (KJV) - "Which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures; Which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave?"

question: How did Job describe his feelings of divine confinement and frustration in Job 3:23?
opt1: As a bird snared in the fowler's net whose wings are broken
opt2: As a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in
opt3: As a wild ass bound with cords and cast into a deep pit
opt4: As a traveler lost in the desert when all stars are darkened
correct: As a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in
explanation: Earlier Satan complained God hedged Job for protection (1:10); now Job laments that God has hedged him into suffering with no way out. Job 3:23 (KJV) - "Why is light given to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in?"

question: What striking metaphor did Job use to describe the incessant, overwhelming flow of his grief?
opt1: His tears were as heavy as the sands of the Red Sea, and his groaning shook the pillars of his house
opt2: His sorrow was hotter than the coals of the juniper, and his grief rose like smoke from the altar
opt3: His sighing came before he ate, and his roarings were poured out like the waters
opt4: His weeping surpassed the rains of autumn, and his spirit was bruised like a trampled reed
correct: His sighing came before he ate, and his roarings were poured out like the waters
explanation: Job's agony superseded physical sustenance, with uncontainable cries gushing forth like unstoppable torrents of water. Job 3:24 (KJV) - "For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters."

question: With what terrifying realization of fulfilled foreboding does Job conclude Chapter 3?
opt1: "Behold, the curse of the desert hath overtaken my household, and my hope is perished from the earth."
opt2: "My friends have become strangers, and the shadows of the tomb have encircled my soul."
opt3: "I have looked for light, and behold darkness; I waited for peace, and an overflowing scourge arrived."
opt4: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came."
correct: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came."
explanation: Job confessed that even during his prosperity, he harbored a deep dread of catastrophe; now his worst nightmares had materialized into unceasing turmoil. Job 3:25-26 (KJV) - "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came."

question: Who was the first of the three friends to speak, and how did he tentatively begin his address to Job?
opt1: Bildad the Shuhite; he asked: "How long wilt thou speak these words, and how long shall the wind of thy mouth roar?"
opt2: Zophar the Naamathite; he asked: "Should not the multitude of words be answered, and should a man full of talk be justified?"
opt3: Elihu the Buzite; he asked: "Hearken unto me, for I am young and ye are ancient, yet wisdom is with the Almighty."
opt4: Eliphaz the Temanite; he asked: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?"
correct: Eliphaz the Temanite; he asked: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?"
explanation: Eliphaz, likely the eldest and most respected, initiated the dialogue with polite hesitation before launching into his theological critique. Job 4:1-2 (KJV) - "Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said, If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?"

question: What commendable past ministry of pastoral counseling did Eliphaz acknowledge that Job had faithfully performed for others?
opt1: Job had instructed many, strengthened weak hands, upholden him that was falling with his words, and strengthened feeble knees
opt2: Job had built houses for the poor, fed fifty widows daily, and clothed the fatherless in the gate
opt3: Job had rebuked the Sabean marauders, defended the border of Edom, and offered sacrifices for the city
opt4: Job had written proverbs of wisdom, judged disputes among the elders, and fasted for the afflicted
correct: Job had instructed many, strengthened weak hands, upholden him that was falling with his words, and strengthened feeble knees
explanation: Eliphaz praised Job's historic role as a spiritual counselor who invigorated the exhausted, stumbling, and despairing. Job 4:3-4 (KJV) - "Behold, thou hast instructed many, and thou hast strengthened the weak hands. Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees."

question: What biting criticism did Eliphaz level against Job when personal affliction struck him?
opt1: He observed: "Thou hast boasted of thy righteousness, yet thou art broken like a bruised reed."
opt2: He observed: "But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled."
opt3: He observed: "Thy wisdom hath failed thee, and thy counselors have fled like shadows before the sun."
opt4: He observed: "Thou didst preach faith to kings, yet thou cursest the day of thy nativity like a fool."
correct: He observed: "But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled."
explanation: Eliphaz pointed out the contrast between Job's robust counseling of others and his own present collapse when touched by calamity. Job 4:5 (KJV) - "But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled."

question: What foundational premise of mechanical retribution theology did Eliphaz challenge Job to recall?
opt1: "Consider, O Job, that the Almighty afflicteth whom He loveth, even as a father chasteneth his son."
opt2: "Knowest thou not that the heavens are unclean in His sight, and no flesh can stand before Him?"
opt3: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?"
opt4: "Look unto the generations of old, and see if any man ever trusted in the LORD and was confounded."
correct: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?"
explanation: Eliphaz asserted the dogmatic doctrine that suffering only befalls the wicked; therefore, the innocent never perish or suffer catastrophic destruction. Job 4:7 (KJV) - "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?"

question: What agricultural metaphor of sowing and reaping did Eliphaz invoke to explain Job's calamity?
opt1: "He that soweth sparingly shall reap sparingly, and he that planteth thorns shall gather briars in the harvest."
opt2: "They that sow to the wind shall reap the whirlwind, and their grain shall be devoured by the locusts of the desert."
opt3: "The ungodly are like the chaff which the wind driveth away; they shall not stand in the congregation of the just."
opt4: "Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed."
correct: "Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed."
explanation: Eliphaz maintained that moral causality is as predictable as farming: those who plow and sow evil inevitably reap judgment under God's breath. Job 4:8-9 (KJV) - "Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. By the blast of God they perish, and by the breath of his nostrils are they consumed."

question: What predator imagery did Eliphaz use in Job 4:10-11 to illustrate the sudden destruction of violent, wicked oppressors?
opt1: The roaring of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions are broken; the old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad
opt2: The swooping of the eagle, the claw of the vulture, and the nest of the hawk are cast down from the rocks
opt3: The charge of the wild bull, the horn of the unicorn, and the herd of the forest are driven into the net
opt4: The venom of the viper, the bite of the asp, and the brood of the serpent are crushed under the heel
correct: The roaring of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions are broken; the old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad
explanation: Eliphaz employed five distinct Hebrew words for lions to show that even the fiercest, most formidable predators (wicked tyrants) are broken and starved by God. Job 4:10-11 (KJV) - "The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. The old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion's whelps are scattered abroad."

question: How did Eliphaz authenticate his theological authority in Job 4:12-15?
opt1: He cited the ancient cuneiform tablets preserved by the kings of Teman from before the flood
opt2: He recounted a terrifying nocturnal mystical vision where a spirit passed before his face in deep sleep, making all his bones shake and the hair of his flesh stand up
opt3: He pointed to the unanimous decrees of the seventy elders who judged the tribes of Arabia
opt4: He declared that the angel of the covenant had spoken to him out of the burning bush in Horeb
correct: He recounted a terrifying nocturnal mystical vision where a spirit passed before his face in deep sleep, making all his bones shake and the hair of his flesh stand up
explanation: Eliphaz appealed to private supernatural revelation: a hair-raising, spine-chilling night apparition that imparted an eerie oracle. Job 4:12-15 (KJV) - "Now a thing was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a little thereof. In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, Fear came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones to shake. Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up:"

question: What profound question did the mysterious nocturnal voice whisper to Eliphaz in Job 4:17?
opt1: "Why boasteth the clay against the potter, and why doth the creature question the Creator?"
opt2: "Can a mortal comprehend the paths of the Almighty, or search out His unsearchable judgments?"
opt3: "Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker?"
opt4: "Who is he that condemneth the righteous, and who can stand when the Holy One ariseth to judge?"
correct: "Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker?"
explanation: The core of the oracle established the infinite moral gulf between mortal man (frail 'enosh') and the holy Creator ('Eloah'). Job 4:17 (KJV) - "Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker?"

question: How did the oracle describe God's estimate of the heavenly angels compared to human beings in Job 4:18-19?
opt1: God crowns angels with glory while humans are cast out into the outer darkness like withered grass
opt2: God commands legions of cherubim to execute vengeance while mortals are weighed in the balances of vanity
opt3: God seals the stars with His seal while mortals are swept away by the morning wind into oblivion
opt4: God puts no trust in His servants and charges His angels with folly; how much more in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, crushed before the moth?
correct: God puts no trust in His servants and charges His angels with folly; how much more in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, crushed before the moth?
explanation: If even celestial beings (angels) are imperfect relative to God's absolute holiness, mortals made of frail clay and dust are incomparably fragile, crushed easily like a moth. Job 4:18-19 (KJV) - "Behold, he put no trust in his servants; and his angels he charged with folly: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth?"

question: How did Eliphaz conclude his account of human transience in Job 4:20-21?
opt1: They are destroyed from morning to evening, perishing forever without any regarding it; their excellency is taken away, and they die, even without wisdom
opt2: They flourish like the flower of the field, but when the east wind bloweth, their place knoweth them no more
opt3: Their names are blotted out of the book of life, and their memory is dissolved like dew upon the rocks
opt4: They spend their years as a tale that is told, passing into darkness before their days are fulfilled
correct: They are destroyed from morning to evening, perishing forever without any regarding it; their excellency is taken away, and they die, even without wisdom
explanation: Human mortality is depicted as brief as a single day (morning to evening), dying without grasping ultimate wisdom. Job 4:20-21 (KJV) - "They are destroyed from morning to evening: they perish for ever without any regarding it. Doth not their excellency which is in them go away? they die, even without wisdom."

question: How did Eliphaz challenge Job to seek intercession in Job 5:1, and what did he warn concerning wrath and envy?
opt1: He asked, "to which of the saints wilt thou turn?" warning that "wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one."
opt2: He asked, "who among the priests can plead for thee?" warning that pride goeth before destruction
opt3: He asked, "which of the angels can stay the hand of God?" warning that rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft
opt4: He asked, "can the elders of Teman justify thy cause?" warning that impatience provoketh divine indignation
correct: He asked, "to which of the saints wilt thou turn?" warning that "wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one."
explanation: Eliphaz warned that no holy one (angel or saint) would validate Job's complaint, and that harboring anger against God's providence is self-destructive folly. Job 5:1-2 (KJV) - "Call now, if there be any that will answer thee; and to which of the saints wilt thou turn? For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one."

question: What fate did Eliphaz claim to have observed overtaking the children and substance of the foolish man?
opt1: His sons are carried captive into Egypt, his daughters sold into servitude, and his cattle drowned in the sea
opt2: His children are far from safety, crushed in the gate without a deliverer; the hungry eateth up his harvest even out of the thorns, and the robber swalloweth up their substance
opt3: His household is consumed by a famine, his vineyards scorched by fire, and his name blotted out from the gate
opt4: His family dieth by the sword, his tents are overturned by the whirlwind, and his heritage given to strangers
correct: His children are far from safety, crushed in the gate without a deliverer; the hungry eateth up his harvest even out of the thorns, and the robber swalloweth up their substance
explanation: In an insensitive allusion to the death of Job's children, Eliphaz claimed the children of the wicked are crushed in the city gate and their wealth plundered. Job 5:4-5 (KJV) - "His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, neither is there any to deliver them. Whose harvest the hungry eateth up, and taketh it even out of the thorns, and the robber swalloweth up their substance."

question: What universal truth concerning human suffering did Eliphaz proclaim in Job 5:6-7?
opt1: "For God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doers; man drinketh iniquity like water."
opt2: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; yet is their strength labour and sorrow, passing as the wind."
opt3: "Although affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth trouble spring out of the ground; Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward."
opt4: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked; for their heart is like the troubled sea that casteth up mire."
correct: "Although affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth trouble spring out of the ground; Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward."
explanation: Suffering is not accidental or emerging spontaneously from soil, but inherent to fallen human existence, as natural and inevitable as sparks flying heavenward from a flame. Job 5:6-7 (KJV) - "Although affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth trouble spring out of the ground; Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward."

question: What course of action did Eliphaz advise Job to take regarding his dispute in Job 5:8-9?
opt1: To fast forty days in sackcloth and offer seven bullocks at the sanctuary of Teman
opt2: To confess his secret sins before the council of the three friends and ask their absolution
opt3: To write a formal bill of complaint and lay it upon the altar of burnt offering
opt4: To seek unto God and commit his cause unto Him, who doeth great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number
correct: To seek unto God and commit his cause unto Him, who doeth great things and unsearchable, marvelous things without number
explanation: Eliphaz urged Job to surrender his grievance into the hands of the omnipotent God whose wonders are beyond human calculation. Job 5:8-9 (KJV) - "I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause: Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number:"

question: How did Eliphaz celebrate God's providential defeat of the crafty and arrogant in Job 5:12-14?
opt1: God disappointeth the devices of the crafty so their hands cannot perform their enterprise; He taketh the wise in their own craftiness, so they meet darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday
opt2: God sendeth thunderbolts upon their towers, breaking their chariots and scattering their counselors like dust
opt3: God striketh the proud with madness, turning their tongues to confusion and casting their princes into the pit
opt4: God overturneth their thrones in the night season, delivering their palaces into the hands of the barbarian tribes
correct: God disappointeth the devices of the crafty so their hands cannot perform their enterprise; He taketh the wise in their own craftiness, so they meet darkness in the daytime and grope at noonday
explanation: God ensnares the cunning in their own schemes (quoted by Paul in 1 Cor 3:19), leaving them spiritually disoriented like blind men groping at high noon. Job 5:12-14 (KJV) - "He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise. He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong. They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night."

question: With what renowned beatitude concerning divine discipline did Eliphaz admonish Job in Job 5:17?
opt1: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners."
opt2: "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty."
opt3: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered by the blood of the covenant."
opt4: "Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding from the Holy One."
correct: "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty."
explanation: Eliphaz framed Job's agony as paternal corrective chastening, echoing Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-6. Job 5:17 (KJV) - "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty:"

question: What paradoxical description of God's wounding and healing ministry did Eliphaz provide in Job 5:18?
opt1: "For His wrath endureth but a moment; in His favour is life, and joy cometh in the morning."
opt2: "For He killeth and maketh alive; He bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up."
opt3: "For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole."
opt4: "For He teareth, and He will heal us; He hath smitten, and He will bind us up after two days."
correct: "For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole."
explanation: God is portrayed as both the surgeon who inflicts the painful wound and the physician whose tender hands bind and heal the patient. Job 5:18 (KJV) - "For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole."

question: What graded numerical promise of divine deliverance did Eliphaz declare to Job in Job 5:19?
opt1: "He shall preserve thee from three perils: yea, in four shall His right hand sustain thee."
opt2: "He shall redeem thee ten times: yea, seventy times seven shall His mercy shield thy soul."
opt3: "He shall guide thee through forty years: yea, in fifty generations shall thy seed be established."
opt4: "He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee."
correct: "He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee."
explanation: Using Hebrew graded numerical parallelism (six ... seven), Eliphaz promised comprehensive protection from every conceivable calamity. Job 5:19 (KJV) - "He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee."

question: What cosmic reconciliation with nature did Eliphaz promise if Job accepted divine correction in Job 5:23?
opt1: He would be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field would be at peace with him
opt2: The clouds of heaven would drop down fatness, and the desert would blossom as the rose
opt3: The rivers would yield gold of Ophir, and the cedar trees would bow before his tent
opt4: The lions of the forest would guard his flocks, and the eagles would bring him bread
correct: He would be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field would be at peace with him
explanation: Repentance would restore Edenic harmony with the physical creation: inanimate agricultural stones and wild predatory beasts would become peaceful allies. Job 5:23 (KJV) - "For thou shalt be in league with the stones of the field: and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee."

question: What agricultural metaphor did Eliphaz use to describe a peaceful, full-orbed death in old age in Job 5:26?
opt1: "Thou shalt fall asleep like a fruitful vine whose grapes are fully gathered into the winepress."
opt2: "Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season."
opt3: "Thou shalt rest like an ancient cedar of Lebanon that hath finished its century of glory."
opt4: "Thou shalt depart like an olive branch heavy with fruit under the gentle autumn sun."
correct: "Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season."
explanation: A godly life completed in ripe old age was compared to a fully matured sheaf/shock of grain harvested in its proper agricultural season. Job 5:26 (KJV) - "Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season."

question: How did Job describe the weight of his grief and calamity in his reply to Eliphaz in Job 6:2-3?
opt1: He declared his sorrow heavier than the mountains of Edom, causing his tongue to cleave to his jaws
opt2: He wished his grief were weighed in the balances, declaring it heavier than the sand of the sea, which caused his words to be swallowed up (rash)
opt3: He wished his pain were measured against the rocks of Sinai, explaining why he cried aloud in the night
opt4: He stated his calamity surpassed the waters of the great deep, justifying his refusal to eat
correct: He wished his grief were weighed in the balances, declaring it heavier than the sand of the sea, which caused his words to be swallowed up (rash)
explanation: Job explained that his seemingly wild, rash lamentations were driven by suffering heavier than all the sands of all oceans combined. Job 6:2-3 (KJV) - "Oh that my grief were throughly weighed, and my calamity laid in the balances together! For now it would be heavier than the sand of the sea: therefore my words are swallowed up."

question: What vivid military imagery did Job use in Job 6:4 to describe God's assault upon his soul?
opt1: The sword of the Lord had pierced his heart, the shield of his defense was broken, and divine chariots trampled him
opt2: The spear of the Holy One had pinned him to the ground, and angelic archers had encircled his tent
opt3: The arrows of the Almighty were within him, the poison whereof drank up his spirit, and the terrors of God set themselves in array against him
opt4: The iron rod of the Almighty had shattered his bones, and heavenly fire had consumed his dwelling
correct: The arrows of the Almighty were within him, the poison whereof drank up his spirit, and the terrors of God set themselves in array against him
explanation: Job viewed God as a divine warrior shooting venomous arrows into his inner being and deploying armies of psychological terrors against him. Job 6:4 (KJV) - "For the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the poison whereof drinketh up my spirit: the terrors of God do set themselves in array against me."

question: What natural animal behaviors and food analogies did Job cite to justify his complaints in Job 6:5-6?
opt1: The lion does not roar when he has prey, nor does the eagle cry over a carcass; bitter herbs cannot be eaten without honey
opt2: The raven does not croak over fatness, nor does the sheep bleat in green pastures; vinegar cannot quench burning thirst
opt3: The camel does not groan beside flowing springs; sour wine cannot satisfy the hungry soul
opt4: The wild ass does not bray when he has grass, nor does the ox low over fodder; unsavory food cannot be eaten without salt, and there is no taste in the white of an egg
correct: The wild ass does not bray when he has grass, nor does the ox low over fodder; unsavory food cannot be eaten without salt, and there is no taste in the white of an egg
explanation: Animals cry out only when starved; likewise, Job complained because he was deprived of peace, finding his current existence as nauseating as unsalted food or tasteless egg white. Job 6:5-6 (KJV) - "Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder? Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?"

question: What fervent death wish did Job plead for God to grant him in Job 6:8-10?
opt1: That it would please God to destroy him, let loose His hand, and cut him off, finding comfort in not having concealed (denied) the words of the Holy One
opt2: That God would send an angel of mercy to take his breath peacefully in his sleep without further boils
opt3: That a lightning bolt would strike him down before his three friends should speak another word of mockery
opt4: That the grave would open its mouth to receive him so he might join his ten children in the dust
correct: That it would please God to destroy him, let loose His hand, and cut him off, finding comfort in not having concealed (denied) the words of the Holy One
explanation: Job begged God to finish the crushing blow of death, clinging to the clear conscience that he had never renounced or suppressed God's sacred words. Job 6:8-10 (KJV) - "Oh that I might have my request; and that God would grant me the thing that I long for! Even that it would please God to destroy me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off! Then should I yet have comfort; yea, I would harden myself in sorrow: let him not spare; for I have not concealed the words of the Holy One."

question: How did Job describe his physical exhaustion and human frailty in Job 6:11-12?
opt1: He asked, "Am I a giant of the ancient days, or are my bones forged of iron that I should endure?"
opt2: He asked, "What is my strength, that I should hope? ... Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?"
opt3: He asked, "Can a moth withstand the whirlwind, or can a withered leaf resist the desert storm?"
opt4: He asked, "Is my spirit greater than the angels, that I should bear the wrath of the Almighty without weeping?"
correct: He asked, "What is my strength, that I should hope? ... Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?"
explanation: Job reminded his hearers that he possessed vulnerable human flesh and blood, not the endurance of granite boulders or bronze metal. Job 6:11-12 (KJV) - "What is my strength, that I should hope? and what is mine end, that I should prolong my life? Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?"

question: What moral principle of true friendship did Job articulate in Job 6:14?
opt1: "A faithful friend is a strong defense, and he that hath found such hath found a treasure from the LORD."
opt2: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend in the day of sorrow."
opt3: "To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty."
opt4: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity in the presence of the elders."
correct: "To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty."
explanation: Job rebuked his friends' cold legalism, declaring that withholding compassion from a suffering brother is equivalent to abandoning the fear of God. Job 6:14 (KJV) - "To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty."

question: What striking geographical metaphor did Job use to expose the treachery and unreliability of his three friends?
opt1: He compared them to a shifting sand dune in the desert of Paran that blinds the weary traveler
opt2: He compared them to a broken cistern that can hold no water in the day of drought
opt3: He compared them to a morning mist that disappears before the scorching sun of Arabia
opt4: He compared them to a deceitful brook (wadi) that runs black with melting ice and snow, but vanishes entirely when the summer heat arrives
correct: He compared them to a deceitful brook (wadi) that runs black with melting ice and snow, but vanishes entirely when the summer heat arrives
explanation: Job compared his friends to seasonal winter torrents (wadis) that promise abundant water, but evaporate into dry stones precisely when parched summer travelers need them. Job 6:15-17 (KJV) - "My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away; Which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid: What time they wax warm, they vanish: when it is hot, they are consumed out of their place."

question: Which merchant caravans did Job cite as being bitterly disappointed and confounded by these dried-up seasonal streams?
opt1: The troops of Tema looked, and the companies of Sheba waited for them, but were confounded and ashamed because they had hoped
opt2: The caravans of Midian and the camel merchants of Dedan searched for them in vain
opt3: The traders of Tyre and the shipbuilders of Tarshish were shipwrecked upon the rocks
opt4: The merchants of Egypt and the embalmers of Babylon wept beside the dry gravel
correct: The troops of Tema looked, and the companies of Sheba waited for them, but were confounded and ashamed because they had hoped
explanation: Caravans from Tema and Sheba traveled out of their way expecting life-saving water, only to find empty sand, leaving them utterly confounded. Job 6:19-20 (KJV) - "The troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them. They were confounded because they had hoped; they came thither, and were ashamed."

question: What did Job challenge his friends to teach him if they wished to convince him of sin in Job 6:24-25?
opt1: "Show me my transgression in the Law of Moses, and I will bring a sin offering to the altar."
opt2: "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?"
opt3: "Declare unto me the secret wisdom of Teman, and I will sit in silence before the elders."
opt4: "Weigh my words against the judgments of God, and tell me where I have dealt falsely."
correct: "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?"
explanation: Job expressed willingness to listen if they could point out specific, verifiable sins rather than regurgitating vague, speculative theological clichés. Job 6:24-25 (KJV) - "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?"

question: With what scathing indictment of callousness did Job confront his friends at the end of Chapter 6?
opt1: He accused them of stealing his remaining camels and dividing his garments among their servants
opt2: He accused them of conspiring with the Chaldeans and bribing the elders of Uz against him
opt3: He accused them of overwhelming the fatherless, digging a pit for their friend, and treating the desperate words of a dying man as wind
opt4: He accused them of worshipping the sun god of Persia and violating the covenant of Abraham
correct: He accused them of overwhelming the fatherless, digging a pit for their friend, and treating the desperate words of a dying man as wind
explanation: Job condemned their self-righteous heartlessness: instead of comforting a devastated brother, they psychoanalyzed his despair and dug a pit of condemnation for him. Job 6:26-27 (KJV) - "Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind? Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig a pit for your friend."

question: How did Job characterize the universal human condition upon earth in Job 7:1-2?
opt1: As a fleeting dream in the night, with days like a flower that withers before the heat
opt2: As an aimless pilgrimage through a barren desert, with days like water poured upon the rocks
opt3: As an appointed time of hard warfare (hard service) upon earth, with days like the days of an hireling who earnestly desires the evening shadow
opt4: As a wrestling against unseen spirits, with days like a vapor that vanishes at dawn
correct: As an appointed time of hard warfare (hard service) upon earth, with days like the days of an hireling who earnestly desires the evening shadow
explanation: Job depicted human life as grueling compulsory military service ('tsaba' / warfare) or backbreaking hired labor, where the worker counts the hours longing for sunset shade. Job 7:1-2 (KJV) - "Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth? are not his days also like the days of an hireling? As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work:"

question: What horrific physical symptoms of his ulcerous disease did Job describe in Job 7:4-5?
opt1: Burning fevers that scorched his veins, blindness in both eyes, and vomiting gall and wormwood
opt2: Numbness in all limbs, spitting blood, and bones turned black like an earthen hearth
opt3: Inability to speak, paralysis of the hands, and hair falling out like autumn leaves
opt4: Endless tossings to and fro until dawn, flesh clothed with worms and clods of dust, and skin broken and become loathsome
correct: Endless tossings to and fro until dawn, flesh clothed with worms and clods of dust, and skin broken and become loathsome
explanation: Job suffered sleepless torment with open, oozing ulcers that formed crusts of dry dirt, became infested with maggot larvae ('worms'), and continually cracked open. Job 7:4-5 (KJV) - "When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome."

question: What two vivid metaphors did Job use in Job 7:6-7 to describe the rapid fleetingness of his life?
opt1: His days were swifter than a weaver's shuttle and spent without hope; his life was like wind, and his eye would never again see good
opt2: His days were like an arrow shot from a bronze bow; his life was like smoke driven by the storm
opt3: His days were like a runner carrying royal dispatches; his life was like an eagle swooping upon prey
opt4: His days were like a passing cloud over Mount Seir; his life was like dew evaporating from the grass
correct: His days were swifter than a weaver's shuttle and spent without hope; his life was like wind, and his eye would never again see good
explanation: A weaver's shuttle darts rapidly across the loom; so Job felt his painful, terminal days flying by into a hopeless oblivion like an exhaled breath of wind. Job 7:6-7 (KJV) - "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope. O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good."

question: What description of the finality of death in Sheol did Job articulate in Job 7:9-10?
opt1: As the river drieth in the summer drought, so man lieth down and ariseth not till the heavens be no more
opt2: As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away, so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more; he shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more
opt3: As the star falleth from the firmament, so the soul departeth into darkness and is remembered no more
opt4: As the tree is cut down by the woodsman, so man perisheth and his roots are dried up beneath the earth
correct: As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away, so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more; he shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more
explanation: From the perspective of earthly existence, descending into the grave (Sheol) is irreversible; one never returns to inhabit earthly homes or resume earthly vocations. Job 7:9-10 (KJV) - "As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more. He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more."

question: What bold resolution did Job make concerning expressing his inner pain in Job 7:11?
opt1: "Therefore I will lay my hand upon my mouth; I will suffer in silence before the eyes of the Almighty."
opt2: "Therefore I will summon the elders of Uz; I will plead my cause before the judgment seat of the gate."
opt3: "Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul."
opt4: "Therefore I will rend my heart and not my garments; I will weep until the morning star ariseth."
correct: "Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul."
explanation: Given the absolute certainty and proximity of death, Job refused to bottle up his lament, resolving to pour out his unvarnished anguish directly to God. Job 7:11 (KJV) - "Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul."

question: What mythological or cosmic question did Job direct toward God regarding his surveillance in Job 7:12?
opt1: "Am I Leviathan, or Behemoth, that thou bindest me with chains of brass?"
opt2: "Am I Rahab the proud, or the dragon of the deep, that thou shootest thine arrows at me?"
opt3: "Am I a lion of the forest, or a wild bull of the desert, that thou huntest my soul with nets?"
opt4: "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?"
correct: "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?"
explanation: Job asked if he was a chaotic primordial force (the raging sea or marine monster / Yam / Tannin) that God felt compelled to post a round-the-clock armed guard over him. Job 7:12 (KJV) - "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?"

question: How were Job's attempts to find comfort on his bed and couch subverted by nocturnal terror in Job 7:13-15?
opt1: When he expected his bed to comfort him, God scared him with dreams and terrified him through visions, so that his soul chose strangling and death rather than his life
opt2: His couch was consumed by creeping worms, and his pillow was drenched with tears of burning blood
opt3: His sleep was broken by the shouts of Sabean raiders and the howling of jackals outside his tent
opt4: His dreams revealed the spirits of his dead children weeping, causing his heart to fail within him
correct: When he expected his bed to comfort him, God scared him with dreams and terrified him through visions, so that his soul chose strangling and death rather than his life
explanation: Even sleep—the universal refuge of the suffering—brought no respite, as Satanic nightmares and ghastly visions plagued him until he preferred asphyxiation (strangling) to living. Job 7:13-15 (KJV) - "When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions: So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life."

question: With what weary cry of revulsion did Job beg God to leave him alone in Job 7:16?
opt1: "My soul is weary of my life; take away my breath, for it is better for me to die than to live."
opt2: "I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity."
opt3: "Why dost thou contend with a withered leaf? depart from me, O Lord, for I am an unclean man."
opt4: "Hide me in the dust until thy wrath be past; let me sleep with the kings of old."
correct: "I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity."
explanation: Job expressed total disgust with his tormented existence, pleading for God to withdraw His oppressive, relentless scrutiny. Job 7:16 (KJV) - "I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity."

question: How did Job ironically invert the exalted language of Psalm 8:4 in Job 7:17-18?
opt1: He cried: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him, seeing he is crushed like a moth before the blast?"
opt2: He asked: "Why hast thou crowned man with thorns and cast him down from the glory of the angels?"
opt3: Instead of praising human dignity, he lamented: "What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment?"
opt4: He wept: "Why hast thou given man dominion over the beasts, only to make him food for the worms of the earth?"
correct: Instead of praising human dignity, he lamented: "What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment?"
explanation: While Psalm 8 marvels that God visits man to crown him with glory, Job cries out in agony that God's constant 'visitation' feels like relentless, unremitting micro-examination and trial. Job 7:17-18 (KJV) - "What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment?"

question: With what intimate biological plea and theological title did Job address God in Job 7:19-21?
opt1: He begged God to spare him until the blinking of an eye, addressing God as "O Judge of the whole earth", asking why He held him guilty
opt2: He asked for one breath of morning air, addressing God as "O Shepherd of Israel", asking why He drove him into the desert
opt3: He pleaded for a drop of water, addressing God as "O Holy One of Sinai", asking why He hid His face from the afflicted
opt4: He asked how long until God would let him alone till he swallowed down his spittle, addressing God as "O thou preserver of men", asking why God set him as a target and did not pardon his transgression
correct: He asked how long until God would let him alone till he swallowed down his spittle, addressing God as "O thou preserver of men", asking why God set him as a target and did not pardon his transgression
explanation: Job used a graphic Middle Eastern idiom for a split second ('till I swallow down my spittle'), acknowledging God as 'preserver of men' while asking why He treats Job like an archery target. Job 7:19-21 (KJV) - "How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be."

question: How did Bildad the Shuhite open his first discourse against Job in Job 8:1-2?
opt1: He asked: "Dost thou imagine to contend with the Almighty, and shall thy tongue roar like a desert lion?"
opt2: He asked: "Why hast thou despised the wisdom of Teman, and why dost thou utter words without knowledge?"
opt3: He asked: "Can a man justify himself before God, and shall a moth boast against the flame?"
opt4: He asked: "How long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?"
correct: He asked: "How long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?"
explanation: Bildad harshly dismissed Job's heartfelt lamentations as blustering, destructive, empty gusts of tempestuous air ('a strong wind'). Job 8:1-2 (KJV) - "Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, How long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?"

question: What core rhetorical question regarding divine justice did Bildad pose in Job 8:3?
opt1: "Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice?"
opt2: "Can the righteous stumble in the day of adversity, or doth the Lord forsake the upright?"
opt3: "Is there iniquity with the Creator, or can the Holy One of Israel deal falsely with man?"
opt4: "Shall the Judge of all the earth do wrong, or hath the Almighty forgotten His covenant?"
correct: "Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice?"
explanation: Bildad's theology rested on the premise of immediate moral symmetry: God can never distort justice; hence, current suffering must reflect past guilt. Job 8:3 (KJV) - "Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice?"

question: What brutal, callous theological verdict did Bildad pronounce regarding the tragic death of Job's ten children in Job 8:4?
opt1: He claimed that Job's sons had aligned with the Chaldeans and suffered military retribution
opt2: He asserted that if Job's children had sinned against God, God had cast them away for their transgression
opt3: He argued that their feasting had provoked the anger of the desert tribes of Seir
opt4: He declared that God took them away in mercy to spare them from witnessing Job's disease
correct: He asserted that if Job's children had sinned against God, God had cast them away for their transgression
explanation: With shocking insensitivity, Bildad deduced from their sudden death that Job's children were wicked sinners whom God justly discarded for their sins. Job 8:4 (KJV) - "If thy children have sinned against him, and he have cast them away for their transgression;"

question: What conditional promise of restoration did Bildad offer Job in Job 8:5-7?
opt1: If Job would offer forty rams at the sanctuary of Shuah, the angel of healing would touch his ulcers
opt2: If Job would confess his hidden usury, his three friends would restore seven thousand sheep to his pastures
opt3: If Job would seek God early, make supplication, and be pure and upright, God would awake for him, make his habitation prosperous, and his latter end would greatly increase
opt4: If Job would fast for twenty-one days, the Almighty would rebuild his children's houses
correct: If Job would seek God early, make supplication, and be pure and upright, God would awake for him, make his habitation prosperous, and his latter end would greatly increase
explanation: Bildad promised that genuine purity and early supplication would prompt God to revive Job's fortunes, making his latter end far greater than his beginning. Job 8:5-7 (KJV) - "If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty; If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase."

question: To what ultimate authority did Bildad appeal to validate his dogmatic view of divine retribution in Job 8:8-9?
opt1: He appealed to a terrifying dream vision where a spirit spoke to him in the night
opt2: He appealed to an ancient stone stele inscribed by King Melchizedek of Salem
opt3: He appealed to a direct revelation spoken by the angel of the burning bush
opt4: He appealed to the search of the fathers and former generations, noting that contemporaries are but of yesterday, knowing nothing because their days are a shadow
correct: He appealed to the search of the fathers and former generations, noting that contemporaries are but of yesterday, knowing nothing because their days are a shadow
explanation: Unlike Eliphaz who appealed to mystical visions, Bildad appealed to conservative patriarchal tradition—the accumulated ancestral wisdom of ancient generations. Job 8:8-9 (KJV) - "For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: (For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow:)"

question: What botanical analogies did Bildad use in Job 8:11-12 to illustrate the rapid withering of the ungodly?
opt1: Can the rush grow without mire, or the flag grow without water? While yet in greenness, it withers before any other herb
opt2: Can the cedar flourish without rain, or the oak stand without deep roots? It is uprooted by the storm
opt3: Can the vine bear fruit in the desert, or the olive tree yield oil in dry gravel? Its leaves dry up at noon
opt4: Can the wheat grow upon rock, or the barley survive the locust? It is consumed before the harvest
correct: Can the rush grow without mire, or the flag grow without water? While yet in greenness, it withers before any other herb
explanation: Papyrus reeds (rush) and marsh grass (flag) depend entirely on swamp moisture; deprived of water, they wither faster than any other plant, illustrating the hypocrite cut off from God. Job 8:11-12 (KJV) - "Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water? Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb."

question: What fragile image did Bildad use in Job 8:13-15 to describe the confidence and trust of the hypocrite?
opt1: The hypocrite's house is built upon sinking sand, washed away by the first desert flood
opt2: The hypocrite's trust is a spider's web; he leans upon his house, but it shall not stand; he holds it fast, but it shall not endure
opt3: The hypocrite's anchor is made of brittle clay, broken when the sea billows arise
opt4: The hypocrite's shield is woven of dry straw, pierced by the arrows of the archer
correct: The hypocrite's trust is a spider's web; he leans upon his house, but it shall not stand; he holds it fast, but it shall not endure
explanation: Bildad compared the ungodly person's security to a flimsy spider's web: leaning on it for structural support results in total collapse. Job 8:14-15 (KJV) - "Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web. He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure."

question: How did Bildad describe the flourishing and subsequent erasure of a garden creeper in Job 8:16-18?
opt1: It blossoms with white flowers in the morning, but is trampled by wild beasts before the evening
